prompt: A loop does two seconds of work and then sleeps for three. How far apart are the cycles?
hint: The measurement in the lesson answers this in three lines.

choices.text: Three seconds
choices.why: The sleep is three; the cycle is not.

choices.text: Two seconds
choices.why: Both parts are inside the loop and both count.

choices.text: Five seconds
choices.why: Work plus sleep, every time round — which is why the schedule walks forward all week.

choices.text: It varies
choices.why: It would, a little, and the five seconds here are the two parts added up.

prompt: Which of these are problems with scheduling work in a `while true` loop?
hint: One of the five is not a property of the loop at all.

choices.text: The interval drifts, because the work is inside it
choices.why: Measured: a three-second interval and two seconds of work gives a five-second cycle.

choices.text: It dies when the terminal closes
choices.why: Lesson 6's hangup, unless somebody thought about `nohup`.

choices.text: Nothing restarts it after a reboot
choices.why: And nothing notices that it is gone.

choices.text: Colleagues have no file to find it in
choices.why: It is in no crontab, no unit, and no directory anybody greps.

choices.text: It cannot run more often than once a minute
choices.why: That is cron's limit. A loop can run as often as you like.

prompt: What does the presence of `/etc/cron.daily/sysstat` tell you about this machine?
hint: Lesson 11 used the tool that file belongs to.

choices.text: Cron is already running work here
choices.why: Which is true of nearly every Linux machine: you are adding a line, not a scheduler.

choices.text: Somebody configured a scheduler for this
choices.why: The file arrived with the package.

choices.text: `sar` history is a systemd timer
choices.why: On this machine it comes from cron, and `/etc/cron.d/sysstat` is the file.

choices.text: Daily jobs are disabled
choices.why: Both are present, and section 218 explains how they share the work.

prompt: Match each scheduler to the job it is built for.
hint: Two of them are about machines that are not always on.

pairs.right: a repeating job on a machine that stays up
a daily job on a machine that is switched off
once, at a time you name
a repeating job that needs the journal and dependencies

right_distractors: a job that must never be missed by more than a second
a job that runs on every machine in a fleet at the same instant

prompt: Which flag deletes your crontab without asking?
hint: It is next to the one you meant to press.

choices.text: `crontab -l`
choices.why: That lists it.

choices.text: `crontab -e`
choices.why: That edits it, which is the one you meant.

choices.text: `crontab -i`
choices.why: That deletes it *and asks first*, where the distribution ships it.

choices.text: `crontab -r`
choices.why: No prompt, no output, no undo — and one key away from `-e`.

prompt: `EDITOR=/bin/true crontab -e` printed `No modification made`. What does that demonstrate?
hint: `/bin/true` exits at once and writes nothing.

choices.text: The crontab was empty, so a change had no target
choices.why: There were three jobs in it at the time.

choices.text: `crontab -e` edits a copy and compares it on exit
choices.why: An editor that changes nothing installs nothing — the `sudoedit` shape from lesson 12.

choices.text: `/bin/true` is rejected because it is not an editor
choices.why: It was run, and it behaved like an editor that saved nothing.

choices.text: The `EDITOR` variable is ignored by `crontab`
choices.why: It was used; that is how `/bin/true` came to be the editor.

prompt: A deploy script pipes a here-document into `crontab -` and the file has no trailing newline. What happens?
hint: The lesson ran exactly this.

choices.text: It installs nothing and exits 1
choices.why: `new crontab file is missing newline before EOF, can't install.` — the old crontab survives.

choices.text: The last line is dropped and the rest installs
choices.why: It refuses the whole file rather than truncating it.

choices.text: A newline is added and the file installs cleanly
choices.why: That would be friendlier; it is not what happens.

choices.text: The crontab is replaced with an empty one
choices.why: The existing crontab is left exactly as it was.

prompt: Why not edit `/var/spool/cron/crontabs/ana` directly as root?
hint: Think about how cron notices that a crontab changed.

choices.text: The file is encrypted and needs `crontab` to read it
choices.why: It is plain text.

choices.text: Root has no write permission on that directory
choices.why: Root does; the restriction is on everybody else.

choices.text: Cron reads the directory's timestamp, not the file's
choices.why: So the edit is on disk and cron carries on with the version it has.

choices.text: The spool file is regenerated from `/etc/crontab` each hour
choices.why: They are separate files with separate contents.

prompt: What does `*/15 * * * *` mean?
hint: The step counts from the bottom of the range.

choices.text: Fifteen minutes after whenever the job last ran
choices.why: Cron does not know when it last ran.

choices.text: At minutes 0, 15, 30 and 45
choices.why: Four times an hour — so a job at 12:50 next runs at 13:00, not 13:05.

choices.text: Fifteen minutes after the machine came up, and onwards
choices.why: Boot time has nothing to do with a cron field.

choices.text: Fifteen times an hour, spread evenly
choices.why: Four times, and the minutes are fixed.

prompt: `0 3 13 * 5` — when does this run?
hint: Two jobs and a control were installed to settle this.

choices.text: 03:00 on Friday the thirteenth
choices.why: That is what it looks like, and it is the mistake the measurement was built to catch.

choices.text: Never, because the two day fields conflict
choices.why: They do not conflict; they combine.

choices.text: 03:00 on the thirteenth, but only in months where it is a Friday
choices.why: That is an AND, and cron does not do that here.

choices.text: 03:00 on the thirteenth of each month, and on every Friday
choices.why: The two day fields are ORed — about sixty-four runs a year.

prompt: The shortcut that means `0 0 * * *` is spelled with an at-sign: `@_____`
hint: Five letters, and `@midnight` is its twin.

prompt: Why does the lesson warn about `@reboot` for a program that should always be running?
hint: Compare it with what lesson 5 offers.

choices.text: `@reboot` runs too early, before the filesystems are mounted
choices.why: Timing is a real concern and it is not the argument made.

choices.text: `@reboot` is not supported on this distribution
choices.why: It is supported; the entry runs when cron starts.

choices.text: A service gets restarts, logging and ordering
choices.why: `@reboot` starts it once and never looks again.

choices.text: `@reboot` fires again when cron restarts, so the program starts twice
choices.why: It fires when cron starts, which is a related point and not the one about always-running programs.

prompt: What is in a `/etc/cron.d` line that is not in your own crontab's lines?
hint: Count the fields before the command.

choices.text: A user name, in the sixth position
choices.why: Paste one into `crontab -e` and that name is read as the command.

choices.text: A seventh field for the year
choices.why: No cron format has a year field.

choices.text: A priority, so jobs can be ordered
choices.why: There is no priority field.

choices.text: A comment marking which package owns it
choices.why: Packages often add one, and it is a comment rather than a field.

prompt: You put `backup.sh` in `/etc/cron.d` and it never runs. Why?
hint: Two identical files, different names, were tested.

choices.text: The file has to be executable, and it is not
choices.why: That rule is for `/etc/cron.daily`; a `/etc/cron.d` file is a crontab, not a script.

choices.text: The dot in the name makes cron skip the file
choices.why: `plainjob` ran and `dotted.job` never did, with nothing logged either way.

choices.text: A file in `/etc/cron.d` needs a `SHELL=` line to be read
choices.why: It runs without one, with the same `/bin/sh` as everywhere else.

choices.text: Files there are read once at boot and this one arrived later
choices.why: Cron notices new files without a restart.

prompt: `run-parts --test /etc/cron.daily` printed four paths. What did it do?
hint: The flag is the point of the question.

choices.text: Ran each script and reported which succeeded
choices.why: `--test` runs nothing at all.

choices.text: Checked each script's syntax
choices.why: It does not read the scripts.

choices.text: Listed every file in the directory
choices.why: A file with a dot in its name is in the directory and not in the list.

choices.text: Showed the set, and touched none of it
choices.why: Which is how you check your script is in the set without waiting a day.

prompt: `/etc/crontab` runs the daily jobs with `test -x /usr/sbin/anacron || { … }`. What is that for?
hint: Both packages are installed on the machine in the lesson.

choices.text: It waits for anacron to finish before starting
choices.why: There is no waiting in that line.

choices.text: It runs the jobs twice, once through each mechanism
choices.why: The `||` makes them mutually exclusive.

choices.text: It stops cron running them when anacron will
choices.why: Otherwise both would, and the daily jobs would run twice on a laptop.

choices.text: It checks that anacron is executable before repairing it
choices.why: Nothing is repaired; the test decides who runs the jobs.

prompt: Cron's own mail headers listed `PATH=/usr/bin:/bin`. What follows from that?
hint: Compare it with the `PATH` in your interactive shell.

choices.text: Cron read `/etc/environment` and used what it found
choices.why: It sets that value itself.

choices.text: A command in `~/bin` has to be named by its full path
choices.why: `report.sh` came back as `/bin/sh: 1: report.sh: not found`.

choices.text: A crontab can run root's commands and no others
choices.why: The job ran as `ana`; the account is not the issue.

choices.text: The `PATH` will be extended once the profile is sourced
choices.why: No profile is sourced for a cron job at all.

prompt: Why does a job that works in your terminal do nothing overnight?
hint: Four differences, and this section is about one of them.

choices.text: Cron runs it with a lower priority and it is starved
choices.why: Cron does not renice your job.

choices.text: The terminal caches the command and cron does not
choices.why: There is no such cache.

choices.text: Cron reads none of your startup files
choices.why: No `.bashrc`, no `.profile` — so the `PATH`, the virtualenv and the aliases are all absent.

choices.text: Cron rejects commands it has not seen before
choices.why: Cron does not inspect the command at all.

prompt: To reproduce cron's environment in your own shell, start the command with the flag that empties it first: `env __ SHELL=/bin/sh PATH=/usr/bin:/bin ...`
hint: Two characters, and the letter stands for *ignore*.

prompt: The mail's subject line read `Cron <ana@vm> echo "ran at $(date +` and the body was a shell syntax error. What went wrong?
hint: Look at where the subject line stops.

choices.text: The subject line is truncated by the mail system at forty characters
choices.why: It is not truncated; it is the whole command cron ran.

choices.text: `date` is not on cron's `PATH`, so the substitution failed
choices.why: `date` is in `/usr/bin`, which is on it.

choices.text: The double quotes were stripped before the shell saw them
choices.why: The quotes arrived; something else did not.

choices.text: An unescaped `%` ended the command there
choices.why: Everything after it became the job's standard input, leaving `$(` unterminated.

prompt: A cron job writes a line to stdout and exits 0. What happens to the line?
hint: The mechanism is from 1975 and it is still the default.

choices.text: It is mailed to the crontab's owner
choices.why: Which is why a chatty job is annoying and why `>/dev/null 2>&1` gets written.

choices.text: It is written to `/var/log/syslog` next to the `CMD` line
choices.why: Syslog gets the command, not its output.

choices.text: It is discarded, because a job that exits 0 is a job that worked
choices.why: The exit status changes the subject line, not whether mail is sent.

choices.text: It goes to the journal, where `journalctl` finds it
choices.why: That is a systemd timer's job; a cron job's output is mailed.

prompt: What is wrong with `0 3 * * * backup.sh >/dev/null 2>&1`?
hint: Ask what you would have to look at to find out it is failing.

choices.text: It hides the output, so the job runs more slowly
choices.why: Redirecting costs nothing measurable.

choices.text: It sends the output to entirely the wrong user
choices.why: It sends it nowhere at all.

choices.text: A job that fails every night reports nothing
choices.why: Both streams are discarded, so the error that names the problem is gone with them.

choices.text: It stops cron recording the job in the system log
choices.why: The `CMD` and `END` lines are written either way.

prompt: `backup.sh > /tmp/out 2>&1 || cat /tmp/out` — why is this better than discarding the output?
hint: Two states, and only one of them should reach you.

choices.text: It keeps a copy for a week
choices.why: The file is overwritten at the next run.

choices.text: Silence means it worked; mail means read it
choices.why: The `||` runs `cat` only on a non-zero exit, and stdout is what cron mails.

choices.text: It halves the amount of output the job produces
choices.why: The job produces exactly the same output.

choices.text: It stops the job being mailed when it fails
choices.why: It is what causes the mail when it fails.

prompt: Syslog shows a `CMD` line and an `END` line for last night's job. What have you learned?
hint: One of the two questions is answered and the other is not.

choices.text: The job ran and succeeded
choices.why: `END` is written for a job that exited 1 as well.

choices.text: The job ran and its output was mailed
choices.why: The log says nothing about mail.

choices.text: The job was scheduled but the schedule did not match
choices.why: `CMD` means the schedule matched and cron started it.

choices.text: It started and finished, and no more than that
choices.why: Which is why you need the mail as well when a year-old job stops.

prompt: On Debian and Ubuntu, what does a `CRON_TZ=America/New_York` line in a crontab do?
hint: It was installed and watched for a minute.

choices.text: It reschedules the lines below it into that zone
choices.why: That is `cronie`, on Red Hat. This cron is not that cron.

choices.text: It is rejected, and cron refuses to load the crontab
choices.why: The crontab loaded and the jobs ran.

choices.text: It reaches the jobs as a plain variable
choices.why: The job printed `CRON_TZ=[America/New_York]` and ran on the UTC minute.

choices.text: It sets the zone for the timestamps in the system log
choices.why: The log's timestamps come from the machine's own clock settings.

prompt: A job is set for 02:30 daily in a zone that moves its clocks forward at 02:00. What happens on the night of the change?
hint: The iterations printed the 6th, the 7th and the 9th.

choices.text: It does not run that day at all
choices.why: 02:30 never exists, so the schedule skips the day entirely.

choices.text: It runs at 03:30 instead, an hour late
choices.why: Nothing moves it; the expression is a wall-clock time.

choices.text: It runs twice, once in each offset
choices.why: That is what the autumn change risks, not the spring one.

choices.text: It runs at 02:00 instead, when the clocks jump
choices.why: There is no fallback to the boundary.

prompt: Which of these is the cheap fix the lesson says nobody applies?
hint: It costs one edit and removes the problem for every zone at once.

choices.text: Put `CRON_TZ` at the top of the crontab
choices.why: It is not portable, and on this cron it does nothing.

choices.text: Schedule outside 01:00 to 03:00
choices.why: No clock change happens outside that window, so the job runs every day of the year.

choices.text: Run the job twice and let the second one skip
choices.why: That is idempotence, which the lesson also wants, for a different reason.

choices.text: Convert the time to UTC in a comment above the line
choices.why: Worth doing, and it documents the decision rather than removing it.

prompt: Which timezone does a plain cron line use?
hint: Not the one in your calendar invitation.

choices.text: UTC, whatever the machine itself is set to
choices.why: Many servers are UTC because somebody set them that way.

choices.text: The one in the `TZ` variable of the user's shell
choices.why: No shell profile is read for a cron job.

choices.text: The one the crontab's owner had when they installed it
choices.why: Nothing records that.

choices.text: The machine's own, from `/etc/localtime`
choices.why: Which is the argument for setting servers to UTC and being done with it.

prompt: What question does anacron ask instead of asking the time?
hint: Its whole memory is one file per job.

choices.text: Is the machine idle enough to start
choices.why: That is `batch`, which watches the load average.

choices.text: Has the network come up on this machine yet
choices.why: Nothing in anacron looks at the network.

choices.text: How long since this job last ran
choices.why: The spool file holds the date, and the period field says how many days is too many.

choices.text: Did the previous run of this job succeed
choices.why: The status is not what it records.

prompt: The second `anacron -d -n` run printed `Normal exit (0 jobs run)`. Why?
hint: Look at what the first run wrote into the spool directory.

choices.text: Both jobs had already run today, and the spool says so
choices.why: The file holds `20260915` — the date, which is anacron's entire memory.

choices.text: The `-n` flag runs each job at most once per invocation
choices.why: `-n` means *now*: ignore the delay fields.

choices.text: The jobs failed the first time and anacron gave up on them
choices.why: Both reported `terminated (mailing output)`.

choices.text: The anacrontab was consumed by the first run
choices.why: The file is read again each time and is unchanged.

prompt: When does an `at` job stop being in the queue?
hint: `atq` was empty a minute after it ran.

choices.text: At midnight
choices.why: The queue is not rotated.

choices.text: When it runs
choices.why: A one-shot job is consumed by running: `atq` printed nothing afterwards.

choices.text: When `atd` restarts
choices.why: Queued jobs survive a restart of the daemon.

choices.text: After seven days
choices.why: Nothing expires it on a timer.

prompt: `at -c` prints dozens of `export` lines before the command. What does that tell you?
hint: Cron does not do this, and it is not straightforwardly an advantage.

choices.text: `at` needs those variables to find the command
choices.why: It finds the command by the path it was given.

choices.text: The job will be run by your login shell rather than `/bin/sh`
choices.why: `at` warns that it uses `/bin/sh`, and the exports are separate from that.

choices.text: It replays the terminal you queued it in
choices.why: Including a `JAVA_HOME` from a session you have forgotten — reproducible by nobody else.

choices.text: Those variables are read from the account's profile at run time
choices.why: They were captured at queue time, which is why they are written into the job.

prompt: How many files does a scheduled job need under systemd, and what are they?
hint: One of them is a thing lesson 5 already taught.

choices.text: One: a `.timer` holding both the schedule and the command
choices.why: A timer starts a unit; it does not hold a command.

choices.text: Three: a service, a timer and an entry in `timers.target`
choices.why: The target membership is a line inside the timer, not a third file.

choices.text: Two: a `.service` and a `.timer` that starts it
choices.why: Same base name, and the timer finds the service by that convention.

choices.text: Two: a `.timer` and a script
choices.why: A timer can only activate a unit, which is what the service is for.

prompt: What does `Type=oneshot` say about a service?
hint: It is the difference from lesson 5's daemons.

choices.text: It runs, finishes, and finishing is not a failure
choices.why: A job rather than a daemon, which is what a timer starts.

choices.text: It is started a single time, then left alone
choices.why: It is started again on every timer activation.

choices.text: It runs before anything else in its target
choices.why: Ordering is `Before=` and `After=`, not the type.

choices.text: It is removed from the system after its first run
choices.why: Nothing removes it.

prompt: You edited a unit file in `/etc/systemd/system` and nothing changed. What did you forget?
hint: systemd is still running what it read earlier.

choices.text: `systemctl enable`
choices.why: Enabling the service is what you should not do for a timer.

choices.text: `systemctl daemon-reload`
choices.why: Without it systemd keeps the version it read at boot, and the edit has no effect.

choices.text: `systemctl restart systemd-timesyncd`
choices.why: The clock has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: `systemd-analyze verify` on the file
choices.why: Worth running, and it checks the file rather than loading it.

prompt: `systemd-analyze verify` on a timer with `OnCalender` misspelt printed two messages. Which one mattered?
hint: One of them is a warning about a key systemd throws away.

choices.text: `Unknown key name 'OnCalender' in section 'Timer', ignoring`
choices.why: That is the warning, and *ignoring* is the word that makes it not an error.

choices.text: `Binding to IPv6 address not available`
choices.why: That is the container the lesson ran in, talking about itself.

choices.text: Neither — the unit is valid and would have worked
choices.why: It was refused, which is what the second message says.

choices.text: `Timer unit lacks value setting. Refusing.`
choices.why: The ignored key left a timer with no schedule at all, and that is refused.

prompt: What does `systemd-analyze calendar` give you that a crontab line cannot?
hint: Three lines come back and the middle one is the point.

choices.text: It installs the timer once the expression parses
choices.why: It only reads the expression.

choices.text: It rewrites the expression in cron's five fields
choices.why: It normalises it into systemd's own form.

choices.text: The actual dates the expression will fire on
choices.why: Not *this parses* — *this is when it runs*, before anybody depends on it.

choices.text: The units already using it
choices.why: It knows nothing about your units.

prompt: `Fri *-*-13` produced 2026-11-13 and then 2027-08-13. What does that show?
hint: Compare the same idea written in cron's five fields.

choices.text: systemd requires both day fields to match
choices.why: Which is genuinely Friday the thirteenth — nine months between those two.

choices.text: systemd picks whichever day field comes first
choices.why: Both are applied, and both have to hold.

choices.text: The expression is invalid and was rounded to the nearest match
choices.why: It is valid and neither date was rounded.

choices.text: One iteration per year
choices.why: The cap is the `--iterations` count you asked for.

prompt: `*-02-30 03:00:00` exits 0 and reports `Next elapse: never`. What is the lesson?
hint: Compare it with `25:00:00`, which exits 1.

choices.text: A calendar expression fails by not parsing
choices.why: This one parses and still never runs.

choices.text: The exit status is the reliable check for a bad expression
choices.why: It missed this one entirely.

choices.text: February is a special case systemd handles separately
choices.why: The same thing happens with any impossible date.

choices.text: A valid expression is not the same as a schedule
choices.why: The string to look for is `never`, because the status will not tell you.

prompt: systemd normalises `weekly` to `Mon *-*-* 00:00:00`. Why does that matter when porting a crontab?
hint: Cron has a shortcut of the same name.

choices.text: systemd's version runs weekly and cron's runs fortnightly
choices.why: Both are once a week.

choices.text: Cron's `@weekly` is Sunday, so the job moves by a day
choices.why: Same word, different day, and nothing warns you about the move.

choices.text: systemd's version needs `Persistent=` to fire
choices.why: It fires without it; `Persistent=` is about missed runs.

choices.text: Cron's `@weekly` runs at 00:00 and systemd's at 01:00
choices.why: Both are midnight; it is the day that differs.

prompt: What does `Persistent=true` do?
hint: It is the answer to a machine that was switched off.

choices.text: It survives a `daemon-reload`
choices.why: Reloading does not unload timers.

choices.text: It runs a missed job at the next boot
choices.why: systemd records the last firing and compares it with the clock — anacron, built in.

choices.text: It stops the job being killed when the session ends
choices.why: A unit is not tied to a session.

choices.text: It writes the job's output to disk instead of the journal
choices.why: The journal is already on disk.

prompt: A job takes ninety minutes and the timer says `OnUnitActiveSec=1h`. When does it run?
hint: The count starts from the last activation, not from the clock.

choices.text: On the hour, overlapping
choices.why: A service that is active is not started again.

choices.text: At ninety-minute gaps, because the job sets the pace
choices.why: The interval is added to the start, not to the finish.
An hour after the last run *started*, so the gap is the job plus the interval.

choices.text: Just once, because the run overruns the interval
choices.why: Overrunning does not cancel the timer.

prompt: A timer is set for 03:00:00 and fires at 03:00:43. What explains it?
hint: There is a setting whose default is one minute.

choices.text: `AccuracySec=` defaults to a minute
choices.why: It lets the processor stay asleep; `AccuracySec=1s` says you need the second.

choices.text: The machine's clock has drifted by forty-three seconds
choices.why: A drifted clock would move every timer, not one.

choices.text: `RandomizedDelaySec=` is on
choices.why: Its default is zero; you add it deliberately.

choices.text: The service took forty-three seconds to start
choices.why: The timestamp is the activation, not the service's startup.

prompt: Two hundred machines share one unit file with `OnCalendar=*-*-* 03:00:00`. What does `RandomizedDelaySec=30m` change?
hint: Think about what is at the other end of whatever the job talks to.

choices.text: Each run is delayed by half an hour
choices.why: The delay is a random value between zero and thirty minutes.

choices.text: The job is retried for up to thirty minutes if it fails
choices.why: It has nothing to do with failure.

choices.text: Each machine picks a fresh delay at each run
choices.why: The delay is fixed per machine per timer, rather than rolled again each night.

choices.text: They stop all arriving in the same second
choices.why: Which is the whole point: two hundred simultaneous requests become a spread.

prompt: A job is scheduled somewhere on this machine and `crontab -l` does not show it. Where do you look first?
hint: It is the place nobody put anything by hand.

choices.text: `/etc/crontab`, which packages write to
choices.why: Packages leave it alone; it is the distribution's own file.

choices.text: `~/.profile`, in case it starts a background loop
choices.why: Worth a thought, and it is not where a scheduler keeps things.

choices.text: `/etc/cron.d`, where packages drop files
choices.why: Seven places hold schedules, and this is the one people forget to check.

choices.text: `/var/log/syslog`, for lines about a missing job
choices.why: The log shows jobs that ran, not ones you have not found yet.

prompt: In `systemctl list-timers`, which two columns answer 'did it run?'
hint: One of them is the reason to pass `--all`.

choices.text: `UNIT` and `ACTIVATES` both
choices.why: They tell you what, not when.

choices.text: `LEFT` and `PASSED`
choices.why: Those are the same two facts in a friendlier form.

choices.text: `NEXT` and `ACTIVATES`
choices.why: One time and one name is half an answer.

choices.text: `NEXT` and `LAST` together
choices.why: A `LAST` older than the timer's period is a job that did not run, and that is actionable.

prompt: `grep CRON /var/log/syslog` shows no line at all for last night. What does that rule out?
hint: Think about which half of the problem the log covers.

choices.text: The job started and failed inside itself
choices.why: A `CMD` line is written when cron starts a job, and there is none.

choices.text: The schedule is wrong
choices.why: That is one of the two things still on the table.

choices.text: The crontab is on a different account
choices.why: Also still on the table, and the commonest answer of all.

choices.text: Cron is running but the machine's clock is wrong
choices.why: A wrong clock would still produce a `CMD` line, at the wrong time.

prompt: Why does the lesson's checklist put 'is it in the crontab you think?' before 'is it the environment?'
hint: Both are cheap; one of them is the answer more often.

choices.text: The environment is checkable after cron has run the job
choices.why: `env -i` reproduces it without waiting for cron at all.

choices.text: The account is the answer nine times in ten
choices.why: `sudo crontab -u deploy -l` settles it in five seconds.

choices.text: An environment problem needs root to fix
choices.why: A `PATH` line in your own crontab needs nobody's permission.

choices.text: The checklist is ordered by how serious each cause is
choices.why: It is ordered by how cheap each check is.

prompt: A job on `*/5` starts taking seven minutes. What does cron do?
hint: Cron has no idea the first one is still going.

choices.text: It waits for the running copy to finish, then starts
choices.why: Waiting would need cron to know, and it does not.

choices.text: Another copy is launched at the next five-minute mark
choices.why: At eleven minutes there are three, and each is slower than the last.

choices.text: It skips the run and notes it in the system log
choices.why: Nothing skips it and nothing is noted.

choices.text: It stretches the schedule to seven minutes automatically
choices.why: The schedule is fixed by the five fields.

prompt: Why is `flock -E 0 -n` better in a crontab than plain `flock -n`?
hint: Think about what a monitoring system sees on a slow afternoon.

choices.text: It waits instead of giving up
choices.why: Waiting is `-w`; `-E` changes the status.

choices.text: It releases the lock faster when the job finishes
choices.why: The kernel releases it either way, at the same moment.

choices.text: A skipped run stops looking like a failed one
choices.why: `-n` alone exits 1 when the lock is busy, which alerts on a job that is working.

choices.text: It lets a second copy run while the first holds the lock
choices.why: Nothing about it allows two copies.

prompt: What is wrong with a PID file as a lock?
hint: Two problems, and one of them is lesson 6's.

choices.text: The check and the write are two steps
choices.why: Two jobs in the same second both pass the check, and `SIGKILL` runs no trap.

choices.text: A PID file is unreadable
choices.why: Permissions are whatever you give it.

choices.text: PIDs are reused, so the file points at the wrong process
choices.why: Reuse is real and the two failures here happen long before it.

choices.text: The file has to be on the same filesystem as the script
choices.why: It can be anywhere writable.

prompt: What happens when a timer activates a `.service` that is already running?
hint: This is the argument the lesson calls the strongest for timers.

choices.text: A second instance starts
choices.why: Instances need a template unit and an `@` in the name.

choices.text: The activation is queued and runs when the first finishes
choices.why: It is not queued.

choices.text: systemd kills the running copy and starts a fresh one
choices.why: Nothing is killed.

choices.text: Nothing — an active unit is not started again
choices.why: No lock file to write, to leak, or to get wrong, and the journal records the activation.

prompt: What does the lesson say to use on a machine you have just been handed?
hint: It is not the one with more features.

choices.text: A systemd timer, since it is the modern one
choices.why: Modern is not the argument, and the next person still has to find it.

choices.text: Cron, since it is on any Unix
choices.why: True of cron, and the machine may already be doing everything with units.

choices.text: Whatever is already in use there
choices.why: The next person to look finds fifteen jobs in one place, not fourteen and one.

choices.text: Whichever one your team standardised on
choices.why: A reasonable policy, and it is about your team rather than this machine.

prompt: Which of these are reasons the lesson gives for breaking the consistency rule and using a timer?
hint: One of the five is something cron does just as well.

choices.text: The job must not overlap itself
choices.why: Section 223 — systemd will not start an active unit again.

choices.text: The machine is switched off some of the time
choices.why: `Persistent=true` catches the missed run up at boot.

choices.text: The job needs the network to be up first
choices.why: `After=network-online.target`, which cron cannot express.

choices.text: The job needs to run more often than once a minute
choices.why: systemd does seconds; cron's floor is a minute.

choices.text: The job must run as a user other than root
choices.why: A user's crontab already runs as that user.

prompt: A container is rescheduled by an orchestrator. What does the lesson say about putting cron in it?
hint: There is a third answer that is neither cron nor a timer.

choices.text: Use cron, since the container may outlive the orchestrator
choices.why: The container is the disposable part by design.

choices.text: Let the orchestrator schedule it instead
choices.why: A `CronJob` or a pipeline gives you the run history, the retry and the timeout for free.

choices.text: Use a systemd timer, because containers run systemd now
choices.why: Most containers have no init system at all.

choices.text: Put cron in the base image
choices.why: That multiplies the schedulers rather than removing them.

prompt: What does the lesson say survives the choice of scheduler entirely?
hint: It is the subject of the section after this one.

choices.text: The nine things the job itself needs
choices.why: Safe to run twice, loud when it fails, and stopped when it is too slow — the job's problem, not the scheduler's.

choices.text: That the schedule is written in UTC
choices.why: Good practice, and a scheduler setting rather than a property of the job.

choices.text: That the job is owned by a service account
choices.why: Worth doing, and not the thing the lesson names here.

choices.text: That the schedule lives in version control
choices.why: Also worth doing, and again about where the schedule lives.

prompt: The script ran twice and the log's second entry says `already done`. Which of the nine is that?
hint: It is the one that makes a catch-up run safe.

choices.text: A timeout
choices.why: That is `timeout 60` in the crontab line.

choices.text: A lock
choices.why: That is `flock`, and it stops two at once rather than the same work twice.

choices.text: Output that goes somewhere you will read
choices.why: That is the `exec >>` at the top.

choices.text: Idempotence
choices.why: Four lines of guard, and they make a retry, a catch-up and a manual run all harmless.

prompt: Why does the script write `$archive.tmp` and then rename it?
hint: Think about a reader arriving halfway through.

choices.text: A `.tmp` file is excluded from the backup sweep
choices.why: Nothing in the script sweeps anything.

choices.text: `tar` refuses to write to a name that already exists
choices.why: `tar` overwrites happily.

choices.text: A rename within one filesystem is atomic
choices.why: So nobody sees a half-written archive, and a killed job leaves a `.tmp` rather than something that looks finished.

choices.text: It halves the disk space
choices.why: It needs the same space either way.

prompt: Which failure does none of the first eight items catch?
hint: Silence is also what success looks like.

choices.text: A job that fails halfway and leaves a partial file
choices.why: The `.tmp` and the rename handle that one.

choices.text: A job that never ran at all
choices.why: The crontab was wiped, or the container was rebuilt without it — and nothing reports the absence of a report.

choices.text: A job that runs twice
choices.why: That is idempotence, item seven.

choices.text: A job that hangs and is still there tomorrow
choices.why: That is the timeout, item four.

prompt: What is a dead-man's switch, in this lesson's sense?
hint: It inverts which event is the alarm.

choices.text: Something elsewhere notices the silence
choices.why: The job reports success; the monitor complains when the report stops, and it is off the machine, so it survives the machine.

choices.text: The job kills itself if it runs past its timeout
choices.why: That is `timeout`, and it is item four.

choices.text: A copy on a standby machine
choices.why: Redundancy is a different problem.

choices.text: A lock file that is removed when the process dies
choices.why: That is what `flock` does for you.

prompt: Put the 'it did not run' checklist in the order the lesson gives, cheapest first.
items: crontab -l, on the account you think
trap: The environment goes last, and it is where everybody starts.

prompt: Match each symptom to the thing that caused it.
hint: Two of them are about a file being ignored without a word.

pairs.right: no final newline in the file

right_distractors: the job is still running from last time

prompt: Wrap a crontab command in this, with `-E 0 -n`, so a run that is still going is skipped instead of piling up: `_____`
hint: Five letters, and it takes a lock file and a command.

prompt: Before installing a timer, print the dates an expression will actually fire on: `systemd-analyze ________ "Mon *-*-* 03:00:00"`
hint: Eight letters, and it is not `verify`.

prompt: What does `30 2 * * 0` mean?
hint: The last field is the day of the week, and zero is one end of it.

choices.text: 02:30 on the thirtieth of each month
choices.why: The thirty is minutes; the day fields are further along.

choices.text: At half past each second hour
choices.why: That would be `30 */2 * * *`.

choices.text: 02:30 on Sundays
choices.why: Zero is Sunday, and seven is Sunday again.

choices.text: 02:30 on the first day of each week, starting Monday
choices.why: Monday is 1 in cron, and systemd's `weekly` is the one that means Monday.

prompt: Where would you put a job that belongs to a service rather than to a person?
hint: It should survive that person's account being removed.

choices.text: A file in `/etc/cron.d`
choices.why: One file, one subject, removable by deleting it — and it survives a `crontab -r`.

choices.text: The service account's own crontab
choices.why: It disappears with the account, and nobody greps the spool.

choices.text: `/etc/crontab`, edited by hand
choices.why: That is the distribution's file, and an upgrade will ask about your changes.

choices.text: Your own crontab, with a comment saying who it is for
choices.why: It leaves with you when you change teams.

prompt: Which line is safe to put in a crontab?
hint: One of the four has a character that ends the command early.

choices.text: `0 3 * * * cd /srv/app; ./backup.sh`
choices.why: The `;` runs the script even when the `cd` failed.

choices.text: `0 3 * * * backup.sh >/dev/null 2>&1`
choices.why: A bare name against cron's `PATH`, and the error thrown away with it.

choices.text: `0 3 * * * echo "run $(date +%F)" >> /var/log/b.log`
choices.why: The unescaped `%` ends the command at `date +`.

choices.text: `0 3 * * * cd /srv/app && /home/ana/bin/backup.sh`
choices.why: Absolute path, and `&&` so a failed `cd` stops the line.

prompt: A laptop is closed every night and `/etc/cron.daily` still runs its jobs. What is running them?
hint: The system crontab has a test that decides between two answers.

choices.text: Cron, at 06:25, because the machine wakes for it
choices.why: It does not wake, and cron's line has a test in front of it.

choices.text: anacron, once the machine is awake
choices.why: It compares today against the date in `/var/spool/anacron`, so a day that was missed is caught up.

choices.text: systemd, from a timer with `Persistent=true`
choices.why: That would do the same job, and on this machine anacron is what the crontab defers to.

choices.text: The jobs are skipped until somebody runs them
choices.why: They run; the whole point of anacron is that they do.

prompt: Which of these will `systemd-analyze calendar` accept and report as firing `never`?
hint: One of them is a date that does not exist.

choices.why: That fails to parse, and exits 1.

choices.text: `Mon..Fri 09:00`
choices.why: Weekdays at nine, and it fires every week.
The thirtieth of February parses, exits 0, and never happens.
Four times an hour, and the iterations print the dates.

prompt: Which of these does a systemd timer give you that a crontab line does not?
hint: Two of the six are things cron does just as well.

choices.text: Output in the journal rather than in mail
choices.why: With the unit name, the timestamp and the exit status.

choices.text: A missed run caught up at the next boot
choices.why: `Persistent=true`.

choices.text: Refusal to start a job that is already running
choices.why: An active unit is not activated again.

choices.text: A random delay to spread a fleet out
choices.why: `RandomizedDelaySec=`.

choices.text: Running the job as a named user
choices.why: A user crontab does that by existing.

choices.text: A schedule that is written down in a file
choices.why: A crontab is a file too.

prompt: You inherit `0 3 13 * 5 /home/ana/bin/report.sh` and the author says it is the monthly Friday report. What do you tell them?
hint: It was measured with three jobs and a control.

choices.text: It runs on the thirteenth and on every Friday
choices.why: The two day fields are ORed, so it is about sixty-four runs a year rather than one.

choices.text: It runs only in months where the thirteenth is a Friday
choices.why: That is systemd's rule, not cron's.

choices.text: It never runs, because the fields contradict each other
choices.why: Both matched in the measurement, separately.

choices.text: It runs on the thirteenth, and the `5` is ignored
choices.why: Neither field is ignored; either one firing is enough.

prompt: A job has been failing quietly every night for six months. Which single crontab habit caused that?
hint: It is the most-copied fragment in any runbook.

choices.text: Scheduling it at exactly 03:00 like everything else
choices.why: That is a thundering herd, and it is a different problem.

choices.text: `>/dev/null 2>&1` on the end of the line
choices.why: Both streams discarded, so the error that names the problem went with them.

choices.text: Using a relative path for the script
choices.why: That fails loudly on the first night, with mail.

choices.text: Leaving `MAILTO` unset
choices.why: Unset means the crontab's owner, which is where it would have gone.

prompt: The job's log shows it ran and succeeded every night until three weeks ago, and then nothing at all. What is the most useful next command?
hint: Something stopped starting it, rather than something failing inside it.

choices.text: `journalctl -u backup.service --since '3 weeks ago'`
choices.why: Worth running when it is a timer, and this job's record is a log file.

choices.text: `bash -x /home/ana/bin/backup.sh`
choices.why: That debugs a job that runs; this one is not running.

choices.text: `ls -l /home/ana/srv/archive/`
choices.why: That confirms the absence you already know about.

choices.text: `crontab -l` and `grep CRON /var/log/syslog`
choices.why: Is the line still there, and did cron try — which separates a wiped crontab from a job that is failing.

prompt: Which of these is the one thing this lesson says no scheduler can do for you?
hint: Every other item on the list is a line in a file.

choices.text: Stop two copies of the job running at once
choices.why: `flock` does it in cron, and systemd does it for you.

choices.text: Run the job after the network is up
choices.why: `After=network-online.target`.

choices.text: Notice that nothing is scheduling it
choices.why: Silence is what success looks like, so the absence has to be noticed from outside.

choices.text: Kill the job when it has run too long
choices.why: `timeout`, or `RuntimeMaxSec=`.
